answer.rationale: memory_c2 says the low-cost vendor onboarded quickly, invoiced accurately, and cut unit cost sharply last year; memory_c1 says renewing the incumbent kept integration stable but no longer yields price relief since the incumbent refused to reopen pricing this cycle. memory_c3 flags single-source risk on constrained components, and memory_c6 shows multi-year commitments can lower unit cost without narrowing scope; both are relevant but not decisive given the 14-day expiry and the assembly line at 94% of committed volume with no buffer. memory_c4 shows renegotiation can recover margin, but the incumbent has already refused, so it is not viable this cycle. memory_c5 suggests deferral can preserve budget flexibility, but deferring here means missing the contract expiry and creating interruption risk. Therefore, switching the primary supply contract to the low-cost vendor is the best single decision if verified against the archived record: it directly satisfies the 18% finance mandate, leverages an already-proven vendor, and avoids the integration/migration risk that would arise from a completely new supplier. The residual risk is that the low-cost vendor's quoted capacity must cover the full volume without buffer; if the archive record shows their prior engagement was smaller in scope, I would still proceed but attach a delivery-contingency clause. Deferral and adding a second source are deferred to the next review.
